topic: Beyond Arrows: Understanding Abstract Vector Spaces
target_audience: Undergraduate STEM students (Mathematics, Physics, Computer Science)

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Familiar Vector
lecture_lines: We often view vectors as arrows in 2D space.
Adding vectors follows the simple tip-to-tail rule.
Scaling a vector stretches or shrinks its length.
animations: Draw a 2D grid with two arrows, u (#0000FF) and v (#FFFF00), starting from the origin.
Move arrow v to the tip of u (tip-to-tail) and draw a resultant arrow u+v (#00FF00).
Stretch arrow u to twice its length to show scalar multiplication, changing its color to #ADD8E6.

sections.title: The Shift: From 'What it is' to 'What it does'
lecture_lines: Mathematicians define vectors by behavior, not just appearance.
A vector space is any set following eight rules.
If objects follow axioms, they act like vectors.
animations: Display a factory icon (#FFFFFF) in the center with shapes (circle, square, arrow) entering.
Inside the factory, show 'Addition' and 'Scaling' symbols glowing in #FFD700.
Shapes exit the factory; display text 'Follow the Rules' in #FFFFFF above them.

sections.title: The Core Rules: The Axiom Checklist
lecture_lines: Closure means adding two members stays in the set.
Commutativity ensures the order of addition never matters.
Every vector space must contain a unique zero element.
These rules apply to arrows and functions alike.
Axioms provide a universal language for different objects.
animations: Show two arrows u (#00FF00) and v (#00FF00) summing to a vector within a bounded set.
Demonstrate commutativity by showing u + v being identical to v + u using ghosted arrows.
Display a point at the origin labeled 'Zero Vector' (#FFFFFF) that leaves other vectors unchanged.
Split screen: show arrow addition on left and function addition on right (#FF00FF).
Fade to text 'Universal Language' (#FFFFFF) surrounded by icons of arrows and waves [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/waves.svg].

sections.title: Case Study: Functions as Vectors
lecture_lines: Consider functions like sine waves as abstract vectors.
Adding two functions creates a new, combined wave.
Multiplying a function by a scalar changes its amplitude.
Because they follow axioms, functions form a vector space.
This abstraction allows us to treat graphs like arrows.
animations: Draw a sine wave (#FF0000) [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/sine.svg] and a cosine wave (#0000FF) on axes, labeled as vectors.
Overlay the waves and draw the sum wave (#FFFF00) through point-wise addition.
Stretch the sine wave (#FF0000) vertically to demonstrate scaling by a scalar.
Display an axiom checklist next to the waves with green checkmarks (#00FF00) appearing.
Morph a 2D arrow vector (#00FF00) into a sine wave graph (#FF0000) [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/sine.svg] to show abstraction.

sections.title: Visualizing High Dimensions & Subspaces
lecture_lines: Vector spaces can have infinite dimensions, like color palettes.
RGB values act as basis vectors for any color.
Subspaces are smaller planes living within larger spaces.
animations: Show three spheres: Red (#FF0000), Green (#00FF00), and Blue (#0000FF) labeled 'Basis' alongside a palette icon [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/palette.svg].
Blend them to create a new color point in a 3D coordinate system.
Draw a 3D cube and slice it with a translucent 2D plane (#FFFFFF, 0.3 opacity) labeled 'Subspace'.

sections.title: Application: Why Abstraction Matters
lecture_lines: Abstraction lets us treat images as high-dimensional points.
Facial recognition calculates distances between these data vectors.
Linear algebra solves complex problems across many fields.
animations: Display a digital face image [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/face.svg], then break it down into several 'basis images' in #D3D3D3.
Show a high-dimensional coordinate system with two points representing different faces.
Draw a measuring line (#FFFF00) between the two points, labeled 'Distance'.
